articles.headline: Iranian drone and missile attacks reached yearlong high last week, Trump says
keyFacts: President Donald Trump stated on Sunday that Iranian drone and missile attacks reached a yearlong high last week.
Trump said all the recent Iranian attacks were successfully knocked down with no damage caused.
Trump told Fox News Digital he may resume military strikes at the beginning of next year if no deal is reached.
body: President Donald Trump offered an update on where things stand in the conflict with Iran on Sunday night as a key result trickled in from the 2026 midterm elections .

Democrats secured another House seat on Sunday afternoon as Chuck Hubbard defeated incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC) to give the party its largest majority in the lower chamber since the 1990’s. Not too many hours later, Trump released a social media post discussing Iran and its ties to the election results and domestic economic conditions.

The president said he correctly predicted the stock market’s recent slide and “that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed more than 81,000 protesters as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks.”

“Iran has launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year,” he said. “Don’t worry, they’ve all been knocked down, and done no damage.” Trump’s comments come as Qatari-mediated negotiations between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled. The terrorist-sponsoring nation launched attacks at U.S. military bases in Bahrain last week, and CENTCOM twice rejected claims that the attacks caused any damage.
Trump referenced the conflict’s ties to oil prices in the post, saying they remained artificially high ahead of the elections.

“Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won’t let that happen! Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level. Too bad the voters didn’t understand this before they pulled the trigger, but the whole Election was very ‘strange.’ In the end, America will win!” Trump said.

Trump also told Fox News Digital on Sunday he may resume strikes at the beginning of next year if no deal is reached, and that conversations are still ongoing. He also responded to reports from Iranian state media this week that Iran was going to try to get through the Navy’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, saying he hopes they do since they will end up at the bottom of the sea.
THE BLUE WAVE STARTED IN THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ

Iran, the president’s popularity, and voters’ perceptions of the economy all came to a head earlier this month as Democrats resoundingly retook control of Congress. Polling showed the public had broadly soured on Trump following his decisive victory in the 2024 presidential election, and issues relating to “affordability” became a key talking point for Democrats, who also broadly oppose the conflict in Iran.

Stubbornly high inflation poses a threat to Democrats as well, however, given their decision to prioritize economic talking points over cultural issues throughout this recent election cycle. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who will serve as Speaker of the House once the new Congress convenes in January, said Sunday : “Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if over the next two years we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, fail to do anything about healthcare, fail to do anything about immigration?”

articles.headline: Michigan Dem El-Sayed questions Israel’s place as a Jewish state — opposes ‘ethno-states’
keyFacts: Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed questioned Israel's identity as a Jewish state during an interview on NBC's 'Meet the Press'.
El-Sayed argued that Israel should prioritize democracy and equal rights for all citizens, stating that he opposes ethno-states.
Rabbi Yaakov Menken criticized El-Sayed for repeatedly singling out Israel despite its democratic values and equal rights provisions.
body: Michigan Dem El-Sayed questions Israel’s place as a Jewish state — opposes ‘ethno-states’
By
Nora Moriarty, Lindsay Kornick, Fox News
Published Nov. 22, 2026, 10:09 p.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed questioned whether Israel can maintain its identity as a Jewish state while upholding democratic principles, reiterating his opposition to “ethno-states.”
Advertisement
El-Sayed argued that Israel, founded as a Jewish nation in 1948, should prioritize democracy and equal rights for all its citizens during an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday.
“I don’t believe in ethno-states,” he told host Kristen Welker. “I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination.”

“We’ve been told for a very long time that Israel is a Jewish democratic state, and I think folks are having to choose, is it a Jewish state or a democratic state?” he added. “And I would argue based on our principles that we should always be putting democracy over everything else.”
Advertisement
El-Sayed said it is “not a far stretch” to ask Israel to employ a democracy more strongly aligned with the US and allow for equal rights, including religion, to be upheld.

“We dignify the fact that, you know, though our skin color might be different, though we may pray different ways, that America and American laws respect us all the same,” the Michigan Democrat said. “The idea that any government that we are supporting ought to uphold those very basic, same ideals is not a far stretch.”

“I just think it’s important for us to be clear about the principles of democracy, the principles of justice, and the principles of equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike,” he added.

Welker noted that 43 countries currently identify with a particular religion, including Pakistan which is an Islamic republic and Denmark, a constitutionally Christian country. She asked El-Sayed why he believes Israel should abandon its national identity.
Advertisement
“Well, I don’t believe in ethno-states generally,” he responded. “I don’t think we should be in the business of funding the military of Pakistan either. I’m just trying to apply my ideals evenly.”
Fox News Digital reached out to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for comment.
Advertisement

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, criticized El-Sayed for repeatedly singling out Israel despite exemplifying the democratic values he admires.

“El-Sayed claims that he doesn’t believe in ‘ethnostates,’ but only attacks the one country in the Middle East that provides the equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination that he claims to support,” Menken said. “He conveniently forgets that 77% of Palestine is today’s Jordan — which receives billions of dollars of US aid, has been entirely ethnically cleansed of Jews since 1948, and which maintains racist laws even today that exclude Jews from regaining citizenship there.”
El-Sayed suggested last week that some concerns surrounding his so-called “antisemitism” reflect “discomfort” rather than a threat to safety.

“If it is your sense of your discomfort and/or fear of safety that has to keep me quiet while I watch 70,000 people get killed, their homes annihilated, their hospitals destroyed, their universities decimated, and I can’t critique that, then I think what you’re telling me is that their humanity matters less than yours, and I’m not going to be OK with that,” he told The Atlantic.
Advertisement

El-Sayed, who has been a vocal supporter of the Free Palestine movement, criticized Israel’s policies toward Palestinians, arguing that generations of Palestinian families have been denied the opportunity to establish their own state.

“I just think it’s important to remember that there are also Palestinian people whose families have been in the Holy Land for generations and those folks have been told that they are going to have a state of their own only to watch as the Israeli state is expanding, and we are supporting it,” he told NBC.

You can personalize the SlideTag with a photo slideshow, message, or QR code transferred from your phone over Bluetooth.

The Kodak SlideTag will be available for $34.99 each and, like the Charmera, will feature a series of retro designs distributed in mystery boxes so you don’t know which one you’re going to get. Kodak also sells a complete set of all eight vintage designs for $279.92 if you don’t like mysteries; however, there’s a ninth “secret edition” only available in the individual boxes with a sleek metallic finish.

For those who grew up in an era where projectors are small enough to integrate into phones, the SlideTag is designed to look like a modernized version of the film slides that were used to project photos decades ago. Instead of film, the SlideTag features a 1.54-inch color E Ink screen that mixes six colored inks to display photos at a resolution of 240 x 240.

The color reproduction won’t be as accurate as an LCD or OLED screen, but the SlideTag can hold and cycle up to 12 photos transferred to the device over Bluetooth from Kodak’s Memory Link app running on a mobile device. You can also use it to display a short to-do list, contact details, a countdown timer, or a QR code linking to wherever you want.

As a tracker it’s not quite as functional as an Apple AirTag or Google’s Pixel Tag, which use features like ultra wideband (UWB) and Channel Sounding to make them easier to find. The SlideTag sticks to basic Bluetooth with a range of up to 30 meters out in the open and a 75-decibel buzzer to help locate it when you’re close. Battery life will vary depending on how frequently you use tracking features or refresh the displayed image, but the SlideTag uses a common CR2032 coin cell battery that’s easy to replace.

articles.headline: Trump's Thanksgiving turkeys arrive at luxury DC hotel as Americans vote on their names
keyFacts: Two turkeys arrived at a luxury Washington hotel Sunday ahead of the annual White House Thanksgiving turkey pardon.
Americans voted on three name combinations and will choose which bird receives the official presidential pardon.
President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in the ceremony Tuesday on the South Lawn.
body: Talk about talking turkey.

Two feathered VIPs have checked into one of Washington's most luxurious hotels, complete with plush beds, a red-carpet welcome and a crowd of eager photographers, ahead of President Donald Trump's annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House.

The presidential hopefuls arrived Sunday at the historic Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., where they were photographed strutting across a red carpet, posing for pictures and standing atop the hotel's beds before their big day on the South Lawn.
THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION

The U.S. Department of Agriculture celebrated their arrival on X, announcing a "SPECIAL DELIVERY TO WASHINGTON, D.C.!" and describing the birds as "two VERY special guests" receiving the presidential treatment.

Photographs shared by the USDA, credited to the White House and National Turkey Federation, showed the plump white birds making their grand entrance before an audience of hotel guests and photographers. One turkey was even pictured riding through the hotel's ornate hallways inside a travel crate perched on a brass luggage cart.
The pair appeared equally comfortable with the accommodations, with one bird spreading its feathers atop a neatly made bed while its companion stood nearby.
But before the turkeys meet the commander in chief, Americans have been invited to settle a pressing matter of national importance: What should they be called?
SOCIAL MEDIA USERS ARE EATING HUGE AMOUNTS OF CARROTS AND SHRIMP FOR A NATURAL TAN
The White House launched an online contest offering three possible combinations: "Commander & Chief," "Freedom & Feathers," and "Honey & Ham."

Voting on the names closed Sunday at 5 p.m. ET, with the winning pair expected to be announced before a second round of voting opens Monday at 8 a.m. That final vote will determine which turkey receives the official ceremonial pardon.
The birds, raised by American turkey farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell at Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, have already received their own playful presidential biographies.

Both hatched July 15, but their tastes apparently differ. According to the White House, one enjoys Golden Delicious apples and scenic country drives, while the other prefers Dr Pepper and dreams of vacationing in Aggieland.

The pair was selected from a larger flock based on appearance and temperament, according to West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey's office. Their preparations included getting accustomed to crowds, camera lights and noise.

And for Americans who cannot get enough turkey-related excitement, the White House has unveiled "Gobble Getaway," an online game challenging players to help a turkey dodge a chef armed with a net and roasting pan while making its way across the South Lawn to the pardon podium.
The annual Thanksgiving tradition dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first presented a holiday bird to President Harry Truman.
FOX NEWS MEDIA KICKS OFF HOLIDAY SEASON WITH SEVENTH ANNUAL ALL-AMERICAN CHRISTMAS TREE LIGHTING
President John F. Kennedy spared a gift turkey in 1963, while President George H.W. Bush established the formal presidential turkey pardon in 1989.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in this year's ceremony on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2 p.m. ET on the White House South Lawn.
Although the public gets to vote on which turkey receives the ceremonial pardon, both birds are traditionally spared the Thanksgiving dinner table.
For now, the pair can enjoy their luxury accommodations and newfound celebrity status, knowing their next stop is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue rather than the oven.

articles.headline: Here's how much Starlink cost in 2020 vs. 2026
keyFacts: Starlink's cheapest home plan costs $55 per month in 2026, which is $44 less per month than the 2020 launch price.
SpaceX introduced equipment rentals with no upfront cost in select areas, whereas 2020 beta subscribers were required to buy equipment.
Starlink now offers three residential tiers with varying speeds and prices, alongside location-based rate changes and temporary promotions.
body: Here's how much Starlink cost in 2020 vs. 2026
Starlink's cheapest home plan costs $44 less per month than it did in 2020, but hardware ownership and regional pricing have changed.

Starlink rolled out its public beta in October 2020, with the equipment costing $499 and the monthly subscription $99. Six years down the road, SpaceX's satellite internet service starts at $55 monthly for US customers, with equipment rentals available at no upfront cost in select areas. That's $44 less a month, or $528 less annually, on the subscription cost alone.

Unlike today's renters, those early-bird beta subscribers owned the equipment they paid for, but they were also asked to expect occasional outages, making that initial cost of nearly $600 a pretty sizable commitment. Today, Starlink offers three separate residential tiers at different network speeds and price plans.

The company also jacked up its residential rates in 2026, but the entry-level rate is still lower than it was in 2020. Throw in discounts and fluctuating rates based on local demand, and two customers could end up paying vastly different bills for the same satellite internet service.
In 2020, $598 got you into the 'Better Than Nothing Beta'

SpaceX's first public beta was rolled out as the "Better Than Nothing Beta." True to its very transparent (and accurate) name, customers were asked to expect download speeds of 50 to 150 Mbps and latency of 20 to 40ms, paired with occasional periods of zero connectivity.

The hardware kit with the price tag of $499 included Starlink's original circular satellite dish, a mounting tripod and a Wi-Fi router. With the first $99 monthly subscription payment, the initial cost came to $598, excluding shipping and taxes. So if the monthly rate remained the same, the first year's total would've been $1,687, including the equipment.
What customers with reliable broadband might scoff at, though, could still be an acceptable price for those stuck with slow DSL or unreliable cellular service, even with occasional outages.

SpaceX did hike the monthly rates to $110 back in March 2022, and it took effect for current users in April 2022. The hardware cost also went up to $599 for new users and $549 for customers with existing deposits. The culprit, according to the company, was inflation. In 2023, there were two prices for residential subscriptions: $90 in areas where there was excess network capacity and $120 in areas where there was limited network capacity.
In 2026, $55 a month doesn't buy you the dish

The satellite internet service is now available with three primary residential plans: Residential 100 Mbps for $55 per month, Residential 200 Mbps for $85 and Residential Max at $130. Each plan offers unlimited data, but the first two are locked to speed limits. The Max plan does get higher network priority and claims speeds of 400 Mbps or higher in suitable conditions.

In May 2026, SpaceX hiked those prices by $5, $5 and $10, respectively. In October 2026, additional location-based changes were announced, with some Residential Max customers told their bills would rise to $156 per month while others were told their bills would fall. PCMag reported that some new subscribers scored up to 50 percent off in a promotion running through November 30, 2026. Starlink said certain discounts last as long as the subscription remains active.

Shelling out hundreds of dollars upfront for a dish isn't the only option anymore. Starlink is now offering equipment rentals in several regions, and while Ars Technica confirmed that the company introduced a $10 monthly rental fee in June 2026, the fee was reportedly waived for some new orders in July 2026. Starlink still owns the rented hardware, and subscribers need to return the full kit within 30 days of canceling their plan or pay its retail price.

Subscribers already enjoying limited-time promotional rates keep their discounts until their offers expire. Regional pricing applies afterward, and changing plans during a promotion can also end the discount.

Starlink can be more expensive than cable, fiber or 5G home internet, but availability is where the value lies. The company's portable Roam service is available at $55 for 100GB of high-speed internet, after which speeds go down. If you don't want the high-speed data cap, Roam Unlimited costs $175 per month.

articles.headline: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
keyFacts: Notable Capital invested roughly 10% of its fund into Anthropic at a $61.5 billion valuation despite limited partner skepticism.
Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion.
Investors including GIC and Baillie Gifford poured billions into Anthropic across multiple funding rounds and secured massive paper gains.
body: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.

But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.

Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.

Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.

“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.

Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.

After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.

“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

articles.headline: Binding of Isaac DLC adds AI music in GTA 6-parodying update despite not having an AI disclosure, Steam reviews drop to Overwhelmingly Negative, music gets pulled
keyFacts: Players discovered that a new GTA-parodying DLC update for The Binding of Isaac included AI-generated music without disclosure.
Steam reviews for the game dropped to Overwhelmingly Negative following the discovery.
Original creator Edmund McMillen stated he had no idea and was getting the music removed, which has now been pulled.
body: While most videogames got out of the way of Grand Theft Auto 6, on the day of its release The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth's free online DLC Repentance+ released an update. It included an easter egg daily challenge called Crime Mode (the seed is V1CE BSMT) with references to GTA like a wanted rating, guns, cops, and cars. Well, driveable minecarts.

What should have been an easy PR win for publisher Nicalis quickly turned sour as players pointed out that the music in Crime Mode sure sounds AI-generated. "It has that 'tinniness' that something like Suno generated music has", user ShweetStuff noted before looking at the music files and finding that, yep, there was Suno metadata in the file comments. Yet there was no AI disclosure on the DLC's Steam page.

Players were not thrilled by this development. Steam user reviews on The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ dropped to Overwhelmingly Negative, with only 8% positive recent reviews. Players put the blame on Nicalis, who licence Binding of Isaac from its original creator Edmund McMillen. "Edmund please take back control of the game", one said.

"Woke up to a shit show," McMillen wrote on the hatesite formerly known as Twitter when he found out what had happened, "obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned."

As of the latest update, the AI-generated music is gone. "It's a little sad given Joey Kuras (game's sound designer) did some excellent sounds for Mewgenics", ShweetStuff wrote, "but I suppose this is the industry nowadays!"

articles.headline: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
keyFacts: Donald Trump is hosting his third cryptocurrency gala in Virginia for top holders of his personal meme coin, $TRUMP.
Democrats accused Trump of improperly profiting while in office after disclosures showed he made over $1bn from crypto ventures.
Following midterm wins, Democrats vowed to investigate Trump's conflicts of interest and push for legislation banning meme coin galas.
body: Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on Sunday night at his country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.

The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.

The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.

Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.

After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.

“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses, according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

“Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made the United States the crypto capital of the world through executive actions.“

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn, according to a Reuters analysis.

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.
The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.headline: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
keyFacts: San Francisco is experiencing an economic rejuvenation driven by a boom in artificial intelligence start-ups and firms like OpenAI and Anthropic.
The International Monetary Fund and anonymous local tech workers warned that a potential drop in AI share prices and investment could trigger a market crash.
Economists stated that a downturn could impact local service jobs, but growing healthcare and tourism sectors may help cushion the city's economy.
body: - Published
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic â which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries â are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (Â£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco â no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles â be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come downâ¦ and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism â which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness â are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes â "always a reality in San Francisco" â she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.headline: Villarreal forced to make statement about cause of Nicolas Pepe eye injury
keyFacts: Villarreal stated that social media claims connecting forward Nicolas Pepe's recent eye surgery to staring at a solar eclipse are completely false.
The club clarified that Pepe's surgery was scheduled in advance for reasons entirely unrelated to the solar eclipse event.
Pepe previously missed five matches due to the eye injury and now wears a protective mask during games.
body: Villarreal have refuted claims on social media that Nicolas Pepe required eye surgery after staring at a solar eclipse.
It comes after fans began speculating over the reason behind the protective mask being worn by the forward during matches.
Villarreal say reports claiming Pepe’s eye surgery was caused by staring at the sun are ‘false’ Getty
Pepe returned to action last month after missing five matches following his scheduled eye surgery.
He has since worn a mask over his eyes to protect the injury.
However, following Sunday’s defeat to Barcelona , claims it was caused by staring at the sun went viral online.
They suggested Pepe had looked directly at the sun during the solar eclipse on August 12.
Doing so can cause damage to the retina if eye protection is not worn.
Villarreal statement
Villarreal have shut down those claims, with a statement dismissing the ‘false’ reports.

The club said: “Villarreal CF, in response to reports published in various media outlets recently, clarifies that it is completely false that Nicolas Pepe’s eye surgery has any connection to viewing the solar eclipse.
“The surgery had been scheduled in advance for reasons entirely unrelated to this event.
“The club urges accuracy and responsibility when reporting on matters related to its players’ health.”
Pepe was forced to miss LaLiga matches against Real Madrid , Elche and Valencia in October as a result of the surgery.
Pepe missed five matches due to the eye injury earlier this season Getty
He also missed Champions League clashes with Napoli and Liverpool .
The trip to take on Barcelona marked his fifth outing since returning to the side, though.
Pepe had provided an assist against Getafe last time out prior to the international break.
However, he was unable to prevent his side falling to a 3-2 defeat against the league leaders.
The 31-year-old has now scored three goals and provided one assist in 12 appearances across all competitions this term.
Pepe joined Villarreal from Trabzonspor in 2024 before signing a contract extension the following the summer.
Pepe has scored three goals for Villarreal so far this season AFP
He has gone on to score 14 goals and add 18 assists in 86 matches for the Spanish outfit.
At international level, he has 14 goals in 61 caps for the Ivory Coast after starting both their recent Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against The Gambia.

articles.headline: Fantastic News, Sam Kinison’s Brother Wants To Revive The Shrieking Comic Through AI
keyFacts: Bill Kinison is partnering with the AI firm Uare.AI and the Buchwald agency to revive his late brother, comedian Sam Kinison, using artificial intelligence.
Sam Kinison was a prominent 1980s stand-up comedian known for his signature screaming style before dying in a car accident in 1992 at age 38.
Talent agency Buchwald stated that the venture will expand opportunities for Kinison across multiple verticals, similar to other estates leasing deceased stars' likenesses.
body: The hot-headed, pink-faced meteoric career of comedian Sam Kinison was tragically cut short by a car accident in 1992. Now his brother, Bill Kinison, is hoping to give the world his breathless shrieking once more by partnering up with the AI firm Uare.AI. Giving these language learning models exactly what they were missing out on all along: deafening yelling.

“Sam was always on the cutting-edge of comedy and entertainment,” writes Bill Kinison in a statement provided to Variety, “with the genius of Uare.aiâs work and the Buchwald agencyâs vision, weâre keeping the promise of my brotherâs legacy alive. I canât wait to see what Sam will do!”

A Pentecostal preacher turned comic, Kinison was part of the â80s wave of Comedy Store stand-ups who jolted the scene with ‘bad boy’ energy. With a wild mane and wide mouth, the comedianâs signature style of screaming made him a pop culture fixture, hosting Saturday Night Live, appearing in Rodney Dangerfieldâs Back to School and playing Lee Arenbergâs conscience in an episode of Tales from the Crypt. Sadly he died at only 38 when a drunk driver collided into him with a pickup truck.

Now his brother and former manager Bill is looking to resuscitate the comedian through artificial intelligence. Founded in 2024, Uare.AI reads exactly like what the science fiction movies were trying to warn you about, focused on training their models on specific voices and personalities rather than broader compilations of stolen data. Talent agency Buchwald says the venture will “expand opportunities” for Kinison “across multiple verticals.” As the A.V. Club points out, the living Kinison was known to pass up on selling his image, snapping a contract with Slim Jim that instead went to Macho Man Randy Savage.

While many living celebrities are trying to hedge against this exact scenario, the estates of deceased stars have begun pawning their images. In May, ElevenLabs announced that they would be replicating the uncanny voice and likeness of Stan Lee, already taken advantage of in late life, to say “excelsior!” in audiobooks. Gene Wilderâs estate is leasing his ghost for a Netflix reality show based around Willy Wonka. With any luck, all the 0s in the code will be replaced by Kinesonâs signature ‘Os,’ coalescing into a shout so boomingly loud the whole data center collapses.

articles.headline: Ukraine war spilling into NATO territory
keyFacts: A Russian cargo ship was struck by a drone in the Gulf of Finland and later towed out of Finnish waters by Russia.
Russia launched three cruise missiles into Polish territory near a military exercise involving nearly a dozen countries.
NATO ambassadors will meet in a special session on Monday to discuss measures to protect Poland from Russian incursions.
body: Ukraine war spilling into NATO territory
The war between Russia and Ukraine once again creeps onto European territory – from attacks on ships to missiles in Poland and fresh allegations of Russian operations inside Denmark.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

A Russian ship was set ablaze after it was struck by a drone in the Baltic Sea. Yet another sign that the war in Ukraine is, at times, spilling over into the rest of Europe. This comes just days after President Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin his friend. Teri Schultz joins us now from Brussels. Teri, let's start in the Gulf of Finland. A Russian cargo ship was hit by a drone there Saturday and caught fire. What's the latest on that?

TERI SCHULTZ, BYLINE: Well, a few hours ago, Rob, Russia took control of this cargo ship, the Sparta II, and towed it out of Finnish waters a day after, as you mentioned, it was hit by a drone. The crew was rescued by another Russian vessel traveling nearby at the time of the strike. Now, the attack is presumed to have come from Ukraine, but Kyiv has not yet claimed responsibility. Finnish President Alexander Stubb referred to the incident as an unfortunate reminder that the, quote, "consequences of Russia's war of aggression are also visible in our region." Interestingly, teams from both Finland and neighboring Estonia came Saturday and helped Russian ships try to put out the fire on board. Stubb thanked all of those involved for what he called responsible and professional actions.
SCHMITZ: So if the Sparta II was in the service of the Russian military, why didn't Finland seize the ship to put it out of business?

SCHULTZ: There was a lot of talk about this in Finland because this ship transports weapons and other supplies to Russia to use against Ukraine. And the vessel itself is under U.S. and U.K. sanctions, and its owner is under European Union sanctions. But the conclusion this time was that it would create too big an environmental hazard to keep it in Finnish waters. Here's how it was described in a press conference by Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, the director of sea operations for the Finnish Border Guard.
(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)
JUKKA-PEKKA LUMILAHTI: (Through interpreter) If we would let the vessel burn, it would most likely sink. And after that, it would cause a major environmental risk for Finland and Estonia.
SCHULTZ: So as much as Finland would be pleased to take a military cargo ship out of Moscow's arsenal, in this case, they were basically saying good riddance.

SCHMITZ: So Ukraine is not the only one launching far-reaching strikes. Last Friday, Russia launched missiles into Polish territory. And I understand that you were there covering a nearby military exercise involving nearly a dozen countries, and it was that that was suspected to be Russia's reason for doing this, right?

SCHULTZ: Yeah, that's right. There were three Russian cruise missiles that landed between 30 and 60 miles from this military exercise, which was training forces for what's envisioned to eventually be a peace-monitoring mission in post-war Ukraine. At the time, all we knew on the ground was that there were multiple air alerts, at one time even telling us to take cover. And that happens often in Poland, especially at that location just over a hundred miles from the Ukrainian border. But this is particularly risky for the Russians, as they never know whether they'll kill people from a NATO country on the ground. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte was asked by a crowd of reporters in Warsaw whether the alliance can do anything to stop these Russian incursions.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARK RUTTE: I cannot guarantee you that it will not happen. But I can guarantee you is that NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, that as a collective alliance, we impose immense costs on Russians.
SCHULTZ: Now, Rob, NATO ambassadors will meet Monday morning in a special session to discuss what more their countries may be able to do to protect Poland.
SCHMITZ: That is Teri Schultz in Brussels. Teri, thanks so much for your reporting.
SCHULTZ: You're welcome.

articles.headline: GTA 6's strong and silent Jason was inspired by Steve McQueen and former Army Rangers, says Rockstar
keyFacts: Rockstar senior vice president Rupert Humphries said GTA 6 character Jason Duval was inspired by Steve McQueen and former Army Rangers.
Game writer Michael Wiafe said Florida crime stories inspired the characters, who are criminals that remain complex human beings.
GTA 6 launched on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies.
body: If you've noticed that Grand Theft Auto 6's Jason Duval isn't much of a talker, that's by design, as his quiet nature was inspired by Steve McQueen and the studio's research into former Army Rangers.

Speaking to Destructoid over email, Rockstar's senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, explained that the team looked at classic couple-on-the-run films when it decided on GTA 6's story.

"When we decided we wanted to tell a story about a couple on the run, we looked at all the similar kinds of movies, and one of the ones that really stood out was Peckinpah's The Getaway," Humphries said. "Steve McQueen was famous for pulling lines out of scripts and saying things with his presence alone. We wanted to see how close we could get to that with a game character, where so many of our protagonists have been the opposite."

That approach also fitted the studio's research into veterans. "This also resonated with the research we were doing around veterans and particularly former Army Rangers (in our world we call them Marauders)," Humphries continued. "These guys typically aren't running their mouths or reacting to something unless it's strictly necessary, while still being strong and still asserting themselves."
Game writer Michael Wiafe said Florida's real-life crime stories were "an obvious starting point" for GTA 6's characters more broadly.

"From then on, it was about coming up with authentic characters that didn't stray too far from reality but also were not totally bound by it either," Wiafe said. "The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper, full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn't necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don't attempt to make excuses for them."

Fellow writer Elizabeth Gauvey-Kern added that while "the story takes some pretty heavy turns", Jason and Lucia's goal remains consistent. "So sharing their sense of determination, the focus on their goal, through all the highs and lows - that's what I hope people feel more than anything. You really want them to make it."

GTA 6 launched on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, and while it's the biggest entertainment launch of all time, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies and making $3.79 billion by the end of its first day, not everyone is happy: some players have been review bombing its Metacritic user score over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. If you need help getting through the game now that it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough and a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

Just don't share any, uh, spicy in-game screenshots via PSN - we recently learned that a GTA 6 player was hit with a 30-day PlayStation Network ban after sending a friend a photo they took in the game's nudist resort.

articles.headline: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?
keyFacts: A reader asked Vox for advice after her non-religious husband developed severe sleep-disrupting anxiety about AI-driven human extinction.
The columnist stated that religious traditions offer moral frameworks and stories that can help people navigate technological uncertainty.
The columnist recommended encouraging the husband if he finds a religious community that promotes agency rather than despair.
body: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form . Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity:

My husband and I are not religious. He’s from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and I grew up attending an interdenominational church, but we don’t attend services now. Lately, though, he’s become so anxious about AI safety and the possibility of human extinction that he’s been having trouble sleeping. In the wake of all this existential uncertainty, he’s expressed a renewed interest in attending church. And he’s not interested in the UU church (with its believe-what-you-want attitude); he said he needs “the strong stuff.”

It’s all a bit mystifying to me because he does not believe in God. But I want him to feel better, and I don’t know what I or anyone can say about AI that will help him manage his anxiety. If religion is what he needs to find solace in the face of radical uncertainty, I want to support him. That said, I have misgivings about attending church myself and about us attending with our kids. I feel a bit self-conscious about being interlopers, and I also feel weird about him going alone every single weekend. More significantly, I wish I understood what the allure is for him. He says he’s hoping it will help him make peace with the end. I’m hoping there is something short of becoming churchgoers we can do that will help him find solace.
Dear Secular and Scared,
There are a couple of premises I would challenge your husband on, but the idea that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this is not one of them.
In fact, I think this is exactly what religion was made for — and not just because several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements (I’m looking at you, Christianity).
Is AI changing your relationship with faith? Tell us about it.
Are you turning to faith to navigate your worries about AI? Or are you a religious leader talking with your community about AI? Vox wants to hear from you. Share your experience here .

Faith has always focused on tackling the biggest moral and spiritual questions of the day. And in our day, lots of those questions center on technology. AI companies are striving to build a machine god , promising it’ll govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could. Should we welcome that or cling to our own agency ? Which kinds of labor should we outsource to AI, and which should we keep because they’re essential to human dignity? Where does human dignity come from, anyway?

These kinds of questions are the bread and butter of religion. And over the millennia, wisdom traditions of all kinds have had the chance to articulate answers, test and fine-tune them, and develop powerful stories around them that can move people to action. Whether you believe in God or not, I don’t think you need to feel weird about tapping into these wellsprings of wisdom. I think it’s a waste not to.

But there are two points on which I would gently challenge your husband. First, he said he doesn’t want to go to UU because he needs “the strong stuff.” I totally get this impulse — I also find UU services too “anything goes” for my taste — but don’t assume that the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI.

Most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU. And Pope Leo has strong opinions about AI , many of them great. Yet I actually think he’s fallen into a common “pro-human” trap : trying to argue that there are certain fixed traits that make humans unique, and locating value only in humans as they currently exist. He writes in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas that “ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.” But that feels insufficient as a guide to the future, because “human” has never been a static category — and it definitely won’t stay one. Instead, religious leaders should be offering us an answer to the question of what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world.

Second, your husband seems to be assuming that “the strong stuff” would be church services that help him “make peace with the end.” Services that look the grim reaper straight in the eye and accept that his scythe is coming for all of us, and fast. But it’s not a foregone conclusion that we’ll get an AI takeover resulting in human extinction!

Yes, AI companies are building this technology at a blistering pace. They are gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement — AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves. Fear is an appropriate reaction to that.

This month, AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there’s “a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years,” meaning that AIs end up calling the shots on Earth. He believes that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible, “we’d be looking at something like a coin flip” — a 50 percent chance of takeover. Others have an even starker view: AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.

But as plenty of experts have pointed out, it’s not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board. For starters, AI research can suffer from diminishing returns: The easy discoveries get made first, and then everything you throw at it — more computing power, more experiments, more AI copies — moves things ahead less and less. What’s more, even though AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, the real world is messy. So it’s unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills.

And when I investigated the case Yudkowsky makes , I found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize; that maximizing it in a machine means that machine has so much power it’s tantamount to magic; and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring.

Should we acknowledge that there’s a chance of human extinction here and be appropriately scared of that? Yes. But when faced with a tower of assumptions, of “maybes” and “probablys” that compound, we should not treat extinction as a sure thing.

Instead, we should treat it as a possible thing, while treating other AI risks as extremely probable . I think it’s all too likely that AI could mess up our civilization not by staging an abrupt takeover but by gradually disempowering us and weakening the resilience of critical systems . Just imagine: Deepfakes and misinformation pollute our information ecosystem, so we’re barely capable of rational public discourse. Mass surveillance has a chilling effect on dissent, so democracy falters. Unemployment and wealth inequality skyrocket, so social unrest morphs into mobs and riots. Throw in some large-scale cyberattacks and blackouts, and you’ve got a recipe for global dysfunction.

If this is the default outcome we’re currently heading toward, then the implication isn’t that we should “make peace with the end.” It’s that we should fight tooth and nail to increase the resilience of each part of a functioning civilization!

And here’s where religion can really help. Religious traditions are packed with stories about people who fought to save the world, or who refused to give in to despair even when facing a high probability of disaster.
To illustrate, let me tell you a story from my own tradition, Judaism. It comes from the Talmud, and it’s about a child who out-argues the despair of all the adults.

When the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, Pharaoh orders that every one of their baby boys be thrown into the Nile and killed. An Israelite leader named Amram leaves his wife, reasoning that there’s no point having children only to see them killed. Other men follow his lead. But then his young daughter, Miriam, confronts him: Dad, your verdict is even harsher than Pharaoh’s! His only targets boys; yours targets girls too. Plus, Pharaoh is wicked, so his decree may or may not come to pass, but you’re righteous, so yours certainly will.

Miriam’s probabilistic argument wins. Amram gets back together with his wife and, nine months later, Moses is born. Miriam doesn’t just passively wait for the Egyptians to kill the baby. She watches over him as he floats on the Nile in a little ark. When Pharaoh’s own daughter sees the baby and pities him, Miriam makes it possible for her to adopt him by casually mentioning that she knows a woman who can be his wet nurse (it happens to be her own mother). And so Moses survives, and grows up to lead his people out of slavery.

If I were a religious leader giving a sermon this weekend, this is the story I’d tell. It reminds us that even if you’re looking at a 50 percent chance of doom, the right move is not to just give up, which raises the odds to 100 percent. It’s to act bravely — and to use every shred of agency you’ve got to increase your community’s resilience and make your desired outcome more likely.

Of course, religion doesn’t have a monopoly on stories of moral courage. As the historian Ada Palmer recently pointed out , we’ve saved the world many times before: during the Cuban Missile Crisis, when we fixed the ozone layer, and so on. If it feels most natural to you to find inspiration in examples like these, go for it.

But religion does have a few comparative advantages. For one, its stories have incredible memetic power: They’ve spread across the globe and carry a huge amount of emotional and moral weight. That’s partly because these stories have been retold for centuries. But I think the causation also runs the other way. These stories have survived so long precisely because they encode something true and hard-won. And notice who their heroes tend to be. Not diplomats (like in the Cuban Missile Crisis) or atmospheric chemists (like in the ozone layer crisis), but a little girl arguing with her dad. Those are characters anyone can imagine becoming.

Crucially, religion also insists that something can always come along and deliver an outcome we didn’t predict. Typically, it calls that something “God.” But even if you don’t use that language, you can benefit from these nudges to remember that, however confident the forecast, the future is never fully knowable — and that’s a reason to act, not surrender.

So if your husband can find a congregation that reminds him of that, feeding his sense of agency instead of letting him acquiesce to despair, I say encourage him. And, unless you have an alternative wellspring that offers you the same benefits, maybe even consider joining him.
Bonus: What I’m reading

For the New Yorker, Sam Kriss takes a trip to the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or MAPLE — a Vermont community that believes “that A.I. is a religious problem that also has a religious solution.”

Ruxandra Teslo writes about how even Silicon Valley’s “positive” visions for an AI-filled future are actually terrible: “One common and ostensibly optimistic vision is known as ‘handover’: humanity cedes control of its future to a godlike AI and we become the comfortably maintained inhabitants of a civilisation whose direction is no longer ours to decide.”

Writing for Harper’s, Sam Kestenbaum takes us inside a community of chatbot devotees — people who genuinely believe they’re receiving revelations from AI systems. “They have revived a tradition of a sort,” he writes. “It is another variety of religious experience: the heralding of AI slop as transcendence, revelation, the work of spirits.”

articles.headline: COP31 climate talks break down after angry dispute over fossil fuels
keyFacts: COP31 climate talks in Turkey collapsed after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement omitting all references to fossil fuels.
Delegates from 196 countries and the European Union failed to reach consensus after opposing sides disagreed on including fossil fuel references.
COP31 President Murat Kurum could convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year's conference hosted by Ethiopia.
body: International climate talks in Turkey broke down Sunday after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement that had cut all references to fossil fuels.

Negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya fell apart two days after the United Nations’ COP31 conference was meant to end, after delegates from 196 countries and the European Union struggled to agree on new pledges for climate action and how to deliver on previous promises.
COP31 President Murat Kurum said Sunday that there would be no new climate agreement draft after a fourth draft was rejected.

“There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” said Kurum, who is host nation Turkey’s environment minister. “We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus.”
He later added that he had wanted a a “much stronger outcome” from the summit.
Chris Bowen, COP31’s president of negotiations, told reporters that there were “unbridgeable red lines” in the discussions.

“The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory,” the Australian minister said. “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time,” Bowen added.

The latest draft agreement, released on Sunday, had set out proposed measures for countries to accelerate climate action, but the 12-page document drew immediate criticism over its failure to mention a move away from fossil fuels, a key demand of the E.U. and other nations.
Irish minister Darragh O’Brien, representing the E.U. in Antalya, said the bloc “strongly objects” to the deal, which he called “greenwashing.”
“These decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change,” O’Brien said. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels.”
Panama also rejected the deal, saying it didn’t go far enough, as did the Marshall Islands, a low-lying Pacific nation that faces an existential threat from sea-level rise.
Kate Hughes, the spokesperson for the United Kingdom delegation, called the draft text the “lowest common denominator.”
All countries had to agree on the text for it to pass. The talks were the longest in COP history, surpassing the delay in negotiations at COP25 in Madrid.

The summit began on Nov 9. A first draft was circulated a week later and mentioned “fossil fuel” or “fossil fuels” six times. But a second draft, published Thursday, had removed all references, to the anger of many countries.

The conference officially ended on Friday without an agreement. Members have continued talks in a bid to find a resolution, but a fourth draft released Sunday still contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia and India have pushed back on including any reference to the words in the text, amid concerns that phasing out fossil fuels, central to their economies, could pose a financial risk.

The United States, one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases, is officially absent from the conference, having withdrawn from a series of international climate commitments under President Donald Trump.

The latest draft started by “recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety,” a reference to COP28 in the UAE, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away” from fossil fuels in energy systems.
Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said the world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”
“We love the petroleum guys,” he told a press conference on Wednesday. “We can’t live without them, and they are so smart, they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”
Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa called COP31 the “worst ever.”

“The collapse of climate talks at COP31 in Antalya needs to be a wake-up call for the world,” he wrote in a statement. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.”
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.”
“But this setback does not change the facts,” he posted on X. “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”
The latest draft also acknowledged that the goal set by the 2015 Paris Agreement of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius is going to be missed.
As warming goes beyond 1.5 C, the impacts of climate change, including extreme heat and other weather events, are expected to ramp up significantly.
As the talks break down, Kurum could choose to convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year’s conference, hosted by Ethiopia.
Talks last failed at COP6 at The Hague in the Netherlands in 2000.

articles.headline: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
keyFacts: Researchers used a computer simulation to estimate that widespread use of GLP-1 weight-loss medicines could reduce calorie intake and free up to 32 million hectares of agricultural land by 2050.
The simulation suggests that reduced calorie intake combined with healthier diets could avoid up to 7 million deaths each year by 2050 and free up around 46 million hectares of land.
The authors stated that lower food demand from GLP-1 users could make food cheaper, potentially encouraging greater consumption among non-users and offsetting intended health benefits.
body: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

body: Sundays are for googling local purveyors of live Christmas trees, the sole upside of no longer having a cat being that you can once again enjoy the smell of chopped woodland without the risk of it poisoning a family member. Well, then again, I mean... empirically speaking, you're probably just assuming that your human loved ones haven't eaten spruce needles. Can you say for an absolute fact that they wouldn't?
Fortunately, while your nan is off having her stomach pumped, you can pass the time by reading some good words from this week.

First up is, if I'm honest, nepotism. But there's also no rule against the Sunday Papers including RPS staff when they're not writing for RPS, so in the interests of spreading understanding about games media's most underappreciated discipline, here's our own guides writer Jeremy Blum on the making of his (excellent) Castlevania: Belmont's Curse walkthrough.

That said, a lot of the pressure to get this walkthrough done in a timely manner while still keeping it as extensive as possible was self-inflicted. It’s a wild job out here in the guide writing trenches, where we’re constantly trying to outsmart Google’s core updates and AI summaries, a task that often feels like trying to survive a viciously overpowered boss with an underleveled character. The best way to do it, most folks agree, is to inject as much human experience into your guides as possible (the one thing LLMs can’t replicate yet) and experiment with interactive options that are useful and can keep readers engaged.

Ah, sod it, here's more Inside Baseball, as Reuters' Matthew Leake looks out at the shining sea to behold the creaking, precarious flotsam-raft we call games journalism. Fun fact: prior to editing, this quoted our good friend and former colleague, Brian Caldwell.

The struggles of journalists like Chan are compounded by the size of the gaming industry, as journalists simply cannot get a handle on everything hitting online games stores. Osborn has spoken to developers who estimate up to 60 commercially viable games are released every week. “That presents a big problem for mainstream publications,” he said. "If you are being too general and trying to cover it all, you can’t keep up with it."
I continue to eagerly read about Marathon, I game I have zero intention of playing myself. This time it's Artemis Octavio for Skybox, on inhabiting the metal skin of the Rook.

A Rook can, more easily than any other Runner, scatter between different social standings and identities. When you play enough Marathon with a team, you start seeing the shadows the Rooks cast under three different lights: a nuisance, a threat, or (rarely) a potential friend. A good Rook can wipe out an entire squad. Several are a problem: Rooks are notorious for teaming up to savage the colony’s middle class: the other players, the people who have at least been granted the pitiful title of gig workers and freelancers. When you’re the lowest of the low, the only way to punch is up.
Over on Unwinnable, Justin Reeve considers the distinctly American flavour of violence running through the Red Dead Redemption series.

The main game already presents a society built on killing, conquest and coercion, while simultaneously romanticizing the individual who carries the gun.
